lead.headline: Auckland's mayor is spending 100 days — and 100 t-shirts — championing the city's startups
lead.byline: Auckland · what the city's 100-day startup push means for the Bay
lead.brief:
Auckland mayor Wayne Brown has launched 100 Days of Start-ups, wearing a different local startup's branded t-shirt every day for 100 days from 3 July to spotlight the city's founders. The campaign builds toward Auckland Startup Week (12–16 October 2026), with the full programme due to launch on 5 August, and is backed by Auckland Council's Economic Development Office, the Auckland Technology and Innovation Alliance and the New Zealand Institute for Advanced Technology.

More than a quarter of the 100 featured startups are tied to the University of Auckland — whose Centre for Innovation and Entrepreneurship says its alumni have raised more than $8.2 billion in capital over 23 years — with early names including retail-crime intelligence firm Auror and medical-device maker Kitea Health. “By wearing these shirts, I want to draw attention to the talent we have right here in our city,” Brown said, arguing Auckland is “punching well above our weight in deep tech, heavy industry disruption and pure Kiwi ingenuity.”
lead.lens: For Hawke's Bay the interesting part isn't the t-shirts — it's how cheap and effective a bit of civic visibility can be for a startup scene. Auckland already has the capital and the density; the Bay has a real but scattered base of around 500 tech firms and the Hi-Tech Hawke's Bay network, and almost none of the national spotlight. The region could borrow the playbook directly: a low-cost, high-visibility local campaign — the mayors, the port, big employers and EIT actively championing named Bay startups — that turns a loose scene into a story investors and talent can follow. The more concrete move is to plug in rather than compete: get Bay founders and university-linked ventures onto the Auckland Startup Week stage in October, where the capital and networks actually are, and use it to pull investment and profile back to the region. Auckland is showing that celebrating startups is a deliberate choice a city makes; the honest question for Hawke's Bay is whether it will make the same choice or keep its best stories to itself.

sectors.name: Artificial Intelligence
sectors.tag: The AI wave — and where a hands-on region can leap ahead of the dabblers.

stories.headline: Kiwis use AI everywhere — and have mastered it almost nowhere
stories.brief: New Zealand now has its first national AI Strategy (“Investing with confidence”), betting on light-touch rules and fast adoption. Yet while 40–80% of organisations use AI in some form, just 2.7% of workers have it embedded in real workflows, and 79% of employers say they don’t know how to train staff — even as 90% expect AI-powered solutions running by 2028.
body: New Zealand now has its first national AI Strategy, “Investing with confidence,” released by MBIE. It is a deliberately light-touch framework that prioritises adoption and application over home-grown AI development, and leans on existing law rather than new AI-specific rules — betting that fast, safe uptake is the quickest route to lifting the country’s stubborn productivity.

The appetite is clearly there — depending on how usage is measured, somewhere between 40% and 80% of NZ organisations say they use AI in some form, according to the AI Forum’s review of adoption studies. But the usage is shallow. Analysis by consultancy Cairn finds only about 2.7% of the workforce qualify as genuine AI practitioners with the technology embedded in day-to-day workflows, and the typical organisation still rates itself at level 2 — “experimenting” — with a median maturity score of 2.4 out of 5.

The bottleneck is people, not tools. Around 79% of employers say they don’t know how to run an AI workforce-training programme, even as roughly 90% expect to be using AI-powered solutions by 2028. New Zealand also sits 37th on the global Government AI Readiness Index as of May 2026, with a stated ambition to climb into the top 30 by 2030 — the gap between enthusiasm and capability that is the whole ballgame.
stories.lens: The gap is the opportunity. If the national average organisation is still merely “experimenting,” a Hawke’s Bay firm that genuinely operationalises AI — not a chatbot bolted on the side, but AI wired into grading, forecasting, rostering or irrigation — leaps past city rivals still dabbling. The region’s advantage is that its problems are concrete: packhouses, wineries, coolstores, logistics and trades all have obvious, repetitive tasks where today’s tools already pay for themselves. The practical moves are unglamorous but decisive — pick one high-volume workflow per business and embed AI properly, lean on EIT and industry bodies to close the 79% training gap locally, and have councils and economic-development agencies treat AI capability as workforce infrastructure rather than a novelty. The honest caveat: a light-touch national strategy means none of this arrives on its own — the pull has to come from the Bay itself.

stories.headline: Microsoft doubles down on NZ AI skills as its cloud build-out ramps
stories.brief: Microsoft has doubled its New Zealand AI skilling target to 200,000 people by 2028 — up from 100,000 — and says it has already trained about 75,000, tying the push to its expanding cloud and data-centre footprint and the country’s AI capability gap.
body: Microsoft has sharply raised its ambitions for AI skills in New Zealand, announcing it will train 200,000 people by 2028 — double its earlier target of 100,000. The programme has already reached about 75,000 participants.

The push is tied directly to Microsoft’s hyperscale cloud and data-centre build-out in the country: as that infrastructure grows, it needs a local workforce able to deploy, secure and manage it. The training spans several strands, including Microsoft Elevate for Educators, Elevate for Changemakers, and a 10K Women programme.

The company frames it as an economic imperative. Its 2025 Work Trend Index found 59% of NZ business leaders believe productivity has to rise, and Microsoft estimates generative AI could add between NZ$76 billion and NZ$108 billion to the economy each year by 2038. “New Zealand is building strong momentum in AI adoption,” said Jane Livesey, president of Microsoft Australia and New Zealand. “However, now is not the time to take our foot off the accelerator.”
stories.lens: Skills are the bottleneck the adoption numbers keep hitting, and Microsoft’s training is largely free and delivered nationally — which makes it a lever the Bay can pull without funding it. The catch is that “national and online” is not the same as “local”: nobody in Wellington will route these places to Hawke’s Bay workers automatically. The concrete move is for Hi-Tech Hawke’s Bay, EIT and larger employers — the port, packhouses, councils — to actively channel staff into the Elevate and 10K Women programmes and build them into apprenticeship and retraining pathways. Done well, subsidised upskilling both lifts local workers and helps draw remote tech talent to the region; done passively, the training flows to the cities that ask for it first.

sectors.name: Solar & Energy
sectors.tag: The renewable boom — and why the sunny, storm-hit Bay has more at stake than most.

stories.headline: NZ quietly ticks past 1 gigawatt of local solar — and businesses now out-panel homes
stories.brief: New figures reported by NewsWire, drawn from Electricity Authority data, show New Zealand's local networks crossed 1,020 megawatts of installed solar as of 30 June 2026, spread across 88,412 connections — a milestone that arrived unannounced sometime in May. Nationally 80,463 homes now have solar, about one in 25 residential connections, up from one in 160 a decade ago, and around 22% of solar connections now have a battery attached. Businesses now hold more solar capacity — 565MW — than every home in the country combined, on 456MW.
body: New Zealand has passed a quiet but significant energy threshold: total solar capacity connected to local lines networks has topped one gigawatt. According to figures reported by NewsWire from newly updated Electricity Authority data, the country slipped past the mark sometime in May 2026, with no ribbon-cutting and no press release to mark it.

The figures, which NewsWire drew from the Electricity Authority's distributed-generation series to 30 June 2026, show 1,020 megawatts of solar installed across 88,412 connections nationwide, and confirm that businesses now hold more of that capacity — 565 megawatts across 7,949 business connections — than every home in the country combined, on 456 megawatts. The one-gigawatt total is more nameplate capacity than Manapouri, the country's largest hydro station at 850 megawatts — though a megawatt of solar produces far less energy over a year than a megawatt of hydro, so the milestone is more about the sheer volume of hardware installed than a shift in the generation mix.

Regionally, the uptake picture is uneven. Auckland has more solar connections than anywhere else — 14,877 of them — yet it sits near the bottom of the table on uptake, with panels on just 2.4 percent of homes, ranking 14th of 16 regions. By contrast, the top of the South Island owns the leaderboard: Tasman leads the country at 9.1 percent, with Nelson on 7.5 percent and Marlborough on 7.0 percent — against Auckland's 2.4 percent — while the wet, sparsely populated West Coast sits last at 1.9 percent. Nationally, 80,463 homes have solar, about one in every 25 residential connections, up from about one home in 160 a decade ago.

Batteries are increasingly following the panels onto rooftops. At least 19,579 solar connections — around 22 percent — are recorded as having a battery attached, and because retrofits don't always show up in network records, the real figure is likely higher. Roughly 369 megawatts of solar was added in the year to June 2026, and at that pace NewsWire suggests the second gigawatt could arrive around 2029 — though the trajectory has been accelerating.
stories.lens: For Hawke's Bay the timing is pointed: the region is only now gaining its first utility-scale solar farm. Lodestone Energy and lines company Centralines have broken ground on a 31.5 MW, roughly $50 million agrivoltaic plant on the Ruataniwha Plains in Central Hawke's Bay — around 49,000 panels expected to generate about 50 GWh a year, with grazing continuing beneath them — and commercial operation is due in late summer 2027. Developers describe it as filling a longstanding gap in the Bay's energy mix, and it is unlikely to be the last: further projects are proposed nearby, including a Helios Energy farm at Ongaonga and larger developments again on the regional boundary. The clearest lesson from the national figures is that sunshine alone does not drive uptake — sunny Auckland ranks near the bottom — so the Bay's real advantage is one it has to choose: councils resourcing fast, predictable consenting for rooftop and farm-scale arrays; growers, packhouses and coolstores pairing panels with batteries to cut daytime power costs and firm supply after Gabrielle-era outages; and local installers and electricians building the workforce so the jobs and network-resilience benefits of this gigawatt milestone land in the region rather than pass it by.

stories.headline: NZ's biggest solar farm just switched on — and it won't hold the title for long
stories.brief: The 150 MW Tauhei Solar Farm near Hamilton energised on 15 July 2026 — nearly 330,000 panels generating an estimated 280 GWh a year, enough to power about 35,000 homes, with Meridian buying 100% of output for a decade. It dwarfs the previous 47 MW record and leads a wave of grid-scale projects racing to connect as costs fall.
body: New Zealand's largest solar farm has come online. The 150 MW Tauhei Solar Farm, on a 182-hectare site near Hamilton in the Waikato, was energised on 15 July 2026, its almost 330,000 panels able to generate an estimated 280 GWh of electricity a year — enough to power roughly 35,000 homes.

Built by UK-headquartered Harmony Energy with backing from infrastructure investor Igneo Infrastructure Partners, the farm has a deal with Meridian Energy to buy 100% of its output for the first 10 years of operation — the kind of long-term power-purchase agreement that makes utility-scale solar bankable. It dwarfs the country's previous record-holder, the 47 MW Lauriston Solar Farm developed by Genesis and FRV near Christchurch in Canterbury.

Tauhei is the biggest of a wave. Grid-connected solar has moved from a rounding error to a fast-growing slice of New Zealand's generation as panel costs fall and consenting speeds up. The Electricity Authority reports that 247 MW of grid-connected solar has been installed since 2023, with solar setting a new half-hourly record of 210 MW on 30 January 2026 and a pipeline of large projects — some 783 MW expected in 2026/27 — racing to connect over the next few years.
stories.lens: Hawke's Bay is one of the country's sunniest regions, which makes grid-scale solar a natural fit — and, with Lodestone and Centralines' Ruataniwha Plains farm now under construction, no longer hypothetical. For energy-hungry packhouses and coolstores, cheaper daytime power is the direct prize; for landowners, a generation lease is new revenue from the same paddock; and after Cyclone Gabrielle severed power to much of the region, local generation paired with batteries is a tangible resilience play. The concrete move for the Bay is to treat Tauhei as a proof point and get the enabling work done early: councils resourcing fast, predictable consenting, lines companies planning grid capacity for connection, and growers and cooperatives lining up power-purchase deals so the next wave of projects chooses Hawke's Bay rather than passing it by.

stories.headline: Sheep graze under the panels — and 32 farms trial solar and batteries
stories.brief: New Zealand's EECA has selected 32 farms for a solar-and-battery trial — its 'Solar on Farms' programme — collectively installing about 3,616 kW of generation across dairy, sheep, beef, horticulture, poultry, nursery and wine operations. Separately, agrivoltaic sites like the Rangitaiki solar farm in the Bay of Plenty already run sheep beneath raised panels, generating power and farming the same land.
body: New Zealand is testing, on two fronts, whether farms can generate power without giving up productive land. The government's Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority (EECA) has selected 32 farms for a solar-and-battery trial under its 'Solar on Farms' programme, with the properties collectively installing about 3,616 kW of solar — systems ranging from 30 kW to well over 150 kW, plus four battery-only sites — across dairy, sheep, beef, horticulture, poultry, nursery and wine operations. One participant, the Balle Bros Group, has paired a 216 kW array on a packhouse roof with a 116 kWh battery. In return for partial funding, the farms will share performance data and host demonstration events to encourage wider uptake.

The more eye-catching idea is agrivoltaics — farming directly beneath the panels. At Lodestone Energy's 32 MW Rangitaiki solar farm near Edgecumbe in the Bay of Plenty, nearly 60,000 bi-facial panels sit on trackers mounted high enough for sheep to graze and move freely underneath, with the operator reporting that roughly 80 percent of grass productivity is retained while the panels provide shade. Lodestone is also trialling strawberry cultivation between the rows, treating the site as a prototype for pairing generation with farming rather than displacing it.

The appeal is dual use of the same hectares: a generation lease or on-farm power on top of ordinary farm returns, sheep doubling as low-cost vegetation control, shade and shelter for stock, and — where batteries are added, as in the EECA trial — a measure of on-farm energy security. For a country wrestling with how to decarbonise without paving over productive land, 'solar and food' is a far easier proposition than 'solar or food.'
stories.lens: This is the solar story that fits a farming region best. Hawke's Bay's sheep-and-beef blocks, orchards and vineyards could earn a second income from generation on land they already farm, with raised panels adding shade and shelter for stock and batteries firming supply on remote blocks. The practical steps are unglamorous but decisive: growers and station owners running the numbers on a generation lease versus rooftop-and-battery ownership; industry bodies and EECA bringing a Bay farm into the next demonstration round so the data is local, not just Bay-of-Plenty; and lines companies signalling where on the network farm-scale solar can connect. Done well, solar vs food becomes solar and food — extra revenue and resilience without taking a hectare out of production.

sectors.name: Connectivity
sectors.tag: Satellites and rural broadband lifting the ceiling on what the back-country can do.

stories.headline: Your phone now texts via satellite across the 40% of NZ that had no coverage
stories.brief: One NZ’s satellite service — using Starlink’s direct-to-mobile tech — now reaches ordinary phones across roughly 40% of NZ’s landmass that had no cell coverage, starting with texting (free on eligible plans) and expanding to data, apps and calling.
body: Large parts of rural New Zealand have never had mobile coverage. That is changing: One NZ’s satellite service, built on Starlink’s direct-to-mobile technology, now reaches ordinary smartphones across roughly 40% of the country’s landmass that sits beyond any cell tower’s range — no satellite dish or dedicated hardware, just a supported handset. One NZ says it was the first telecommunications company in the world to launch a nationwide Starlink Direct to Mobile service.

It launched with text messaging — free on eligible Pay Monthly and business plans — in December 2024, and in its first year carried around 7 million messages to more than 700,000 customers. From February 2026 the service began expanding beyond texting to satellite data, apps such as Google Maps and AllTrails, and WhatsApp voice calling, and rival Spark launched its own competing satellite text service in April 2026.

For anyone who tramps, farms or lives beyond the towers, it turns a dead phone into a working one — able to send a text from a back paddock or a remote hut. It is the connectivity floor rising for the roughly 40% of the map conventional networks never reached.
stories.lens: Connectivity has always been the low ceiling on rural technology, and this lifts it almost automatically — any Hawke’s Bay farmer, forestry crew or back-country worker with a supported phone gets coverage across country that never had it, with nothing the region itself has to build or fund. The honest point is that this is a national telco capability the Bay simply inherits rather than something it has to win. Where the region can act is on top of it: emergency managers should fold satellite messaging into civil-defence planning after Cyclone Gabrielle exposed how fragile rural comms are; farm, orchard and forestry employers can lean on it for lone-worker safety in the hills; and agritech that depends on a signal — smart collars, remote sensors, precision irrigation — becomes deployable across Wairoa, the coast and the Central Hawke’s Bay hill blocks where coverage was never a given.

stories.headline: How Starlink quietly became rural New Zealand’s default internet
stories.brief: Beyond phones, Starlink has become rural New Zealand’s default broadband — around 85,000 connections (roughly 72,000 rural) and about a 27% rural market share, making it the country’s largest rural internet provider. A Federated Farmers survey put satellite use on farms at 36%.
body: Away from the phone network, Starlink has quietly become rural New Zealand’s default internet. In the year to June 2025, SpaceX’s satellite service grew from about 58,000 connections to 85,000 — roughly 72,000 of them rural and 13,000 urban — making it the country’s largest rural internet provider on around a 27% share, as its qualifying NZ revenue jumped 38% to about $101 million.

The shift shows in the paddock data. A Federated Farmers survey found satellite internet use on farms rising to 36%, while traditional wireless broadband slipped to 44% — a clear move toward satellite, even though fixed wireless narrowly remains the most common rural connection. New Zealand now has the highest per-capita satellite broadband adoption in the OECD. Plans run roughly $85 to $170 a month after a mid-2026 price rise, with hardware around $799 upfront.

The upside is fibre-like speed in places fixed networks abandoned — video calls, live data from the woolshed, streaming in the evening. The catch is concentration: an independent report for the Commerce Commission by Richard Feasey warned of a “material risk” that Starlink could become the dominant or monopoly supplier in rural areas, which would make any future intervention difficult, and local wireless providers are already feeling the squeeze — the Bay of Plenty operator Evolution Networks has gone into liquidation.
stories.lens: For the Bay’s back-country growers and coastal stations, reliable broadband is the difference between “someday” and “deployable” for data-driven farming, and it makes rural remote work, telehealth and online education genuinely workable in places fixed lines never reached. That reframes what regional investment should target: connectivity is now largely a solved problem in the hills, so councils and economic-development agencies can pivot to what runs on top of it — agritech, remote tech jobs, rural upskilling. The honest caveat is concentration risk. With the Commerce Commission already flagging Starlink’s monopoly potential and local wireless operators folding, the Bay would be unwise to let a single offshore provider become the only pipe into the back-country; keeping local wireless firms and fibre extension alive is a resilience play worth backing.

sectors.name: Cloud & Data
sectors.tag: The digital plumbing — and the power crunch that makes regional energy strategic.

stories.headline: Mercury buys into Southland's $3.5b 'AI factory' — as locals demand answers
stories.brief: Power giant Mercury NZ has taken a 12.7% stake for US$30m (NZ$53m) in Datagrid NZ, the Singapore-backed developer building a 360MW hyperscale AI data centre at North Makarewa, Southland. The deal — struck as hundreds of locals packed a public meeting demanding Datagrid front up over water, power and noise concerns — shows how gentailers are now buying equity stakes directly into AI infrastructure, not just selling it electricity.
body: Mercury NZ has acquired a 12.7% minority equity stake in Datagrid NZ for US$30 million (NZ$53 million), deepening a relationship that began with the 15-year, 140MW power purchase option the pair signed in March 2026. Mercury chief executive Stew Hamilton has been appointed to Datagrid NZ's board and framed the move as locking in long-duration electricity demand rather than a speculative punt, saying it "bolsters our position alongside an important emerging source of long-term electricity demand."

The investment underpins Datagrid's planned 360MW hyperscale campus at North Makarewa, north of Invercargill — a 78,000 square metre facility that already holds full resource consent and is slated to open in 2028, with a final investment decision expected later in 2026. Datagrid NZ, majority-owned by a Singapore-based parent and chaired by founder Rémi Galasso, bills the project as "New Zealand's first AI factory." Mercury, a 100% renewable generator, cast the deal as a way to pair its wind and geothermal pipeline — including the Kaiwera Downs and Kaiwaikawe wind farms and a Ngā Tamariki geothermal expansion due this year — with steady demand from a single, enormous customer.

The equity round lands as local opposition intensifies. Hundreds of Southlanders packed the Invercargill Workingmen's Club for a public meeting, some left standing in the hallway, frustrated that Datagrid representatives did not attend to answer questions about power draw, noise and water use. "We've reached out in good faith and it's a shame," organiser Kelly Blomfield said. Datagrid has said the facility will rely on free ambient-air cooling rather than groundwater — helped by Southland's cool climate — and that construction will create around 1,200 jobs, dropping to roughly 80 permanent staff once operational, a ratio critics say underscores how little ongoing employment the project may deliver relative to its scale and resource demands.

The transaction is also a signal for the wider sector: it is the clearest example yet of a New Zealand electricity generator taking a direct ownership stake in a hyperscale AI facility rather than simply supplying it. With the government's Invest New Zealand agency talking up the potential to attract $25–35 billion of private investment in data centres, renewables, fibre and transmission over the next five years, expect more gentailer-developer tie-ups as power companies look to lock in the AI boom's biggest electricity customers before rivals do.
stories.lens: Hawke's Bay doesn't have Southland's scale of renewable generation or a hyperscale AI campus on the table, and honestly it isn't going to. But the Mercury-Datagrid deal is a template worth watching: power companies are now treating AI data-centre demand as a strategic asset worth owning equity in, not just billing for. For the Bay, the sharpest lesson is in the jobs math out of Makarewa — a construction boom but a thin permanent headcount — which argues for the region to chase servicing and supply-chain roles (civil construction, fibre, cooling, grid-connection work) around the national data-centre build-out rather than a facility of its own. It is also a reminder that any future Bay-based digital-infrastructure play — cloud-linked cold storage for horticulture, or agri-data processing — will need local generators and lines companies at the table early, because power supply and data-centre approvals are now tightly bound together nationally.

stories.headline: AWS switched on a $7.5bn NZ cloud region — the plumbing under everything else
stories.brief: Amazon's NZ$7.5 billion AWS Auckland cloud region — three data centres — is live, with first named customers including One NZ, Vector and Datacom. On-shore cloud keeps data in the country and lowers the barrier for local startups, councils and agritech to build serious software at scale.
body: The biggest piece of digital infrastructure New Zealand has ever hosted is now switched on. Amazon Web Services' NZ$7.5 billion Auckland cloud region — three data centres — has gone live, giving local businesses and government the ability to run workloads on AWS without their data leaving the country. The region was first announced in 2021 and originally targeted for 2024, opening after construction delays.

The first named customers include One NZ, Vector and Datacom, the last of which will host its own customers' workloads in the region. One NZ chief executive Jason Paris said the local region would let the telco "leverage in-region workloads to support low latency and AI-driven customer experiences," while Vector's Jerry Li pointed to faster local access to AWS services helping "accelerate our vision of creating a new energy future" for the grid. To power the region more cleanly, AWS has agreed to buy half the output of Mercury's 103MW Turitea South wind farm.

On-shore cloud lowers latency and satisfies data-sovereignty rules, and it drops the barrier for local startups, councils and agritech firms to build serious software at scale. The one shadow over the whole hyperscale build-out — here and worldwide — is electricity, which is fast becoming the limiting factor.
stories.lens: Little of this lands physically in Hawke's Bay — the region has no hyperscale data centre and won't get one. But on-shore cloud is a genuine enabler for the Bay's software and agritech firms: lower latency, data kept onshore, and no need to ship sensitive council, health or grower data offshore. The concrete opportunity here is adoption, not construction. Bay startups, councils and horticulture businesses can now build data-heavy tools — yield models, cold-chain tracking, satellite and drone imagery analysis — on world-class infrastructure at a lower barrier than a year ago, and local firms selling to public-sector or export clients can now credibly promise their data never leaves New Zealand.

stories.headline: AI's power bottleneck: the data-centre boom now needs the regions
stories.brief: Globally and in New Zealand, hyperscale AI data centres are running into an electricity bottleneck — power, not chips, is becoming the limiting factor for the AI build-out, with more than US$162 billion of projects already blocked or delayed over grid constraints.
body: The constraint on artificial intelligence is no longer chips — it is power. As hyperscalers pour more than US$600 billion into new AI infrastructure in 2026, the limiting factor has become the electricity to run it, with grid capacity now dictating where and how fast data centres can be built.

The demand is staggering: analysts expect total hyperscale capacity to double in about three years, against a global pipeline of some 770 planned facilities — on top of nearly 1,300 already operating — that will need "tens of gigawatts" of aggregate power over the next two to three years. It is already biting: as of mid-2025, more than 36 projects representing US$162 billion of investment were blocked or significantly delayed over power constraints and local opposition, and analysts warn grid outages will become more common.

Operators are scrambling for workarounds: on-site generation to skip grid queues, closed-loop liquid cooling (as in Microsoft's Fairwater campuses) to cut water use and strain, and long-term renewable deals. The upshot is a strategic reordering — the regions and countries that can supply abundant clean power become the ones that win the data centres.
stories.lens: This is the national backdrop to Hawke's Bay's solar push. New Zealand won't attract the biggest AI campuses without abundant, firm, clean power, and the regions that can generate it become strategically valuable in an AI-hungry economy. The honest read for the Bay is that it won't host a hyperscaler itself — but its sunshine and emerging renewable pipeline are exactly the kind of asset this reordering rewards, and the grid-connection, construction and servicing work that follows generation is where the regional jobs actually sit. The concrete move is to treat firm regional power as an economic asset, not just an emissions play: councils weighing consents for solar and grid upgrades should recognise that spare clean generation is now a magnet for investment, and accelerating it is how the Bay stays on the right side of this shift.

sectors.name: Space
sectors.tag: New Zealand’s launch industry — with its pad inside the Hawke’s Bay region.

stories.headline: Rocket Lab's $266M Alaska deal shows why NZ's rocket industry still matters to the Pentagon
stories.brief: Rocket Lab has won a $266 million firm-fixed-price U.S. Space Force contract for 12 suborbital HASTE launches from Alaska through 2028, with options for six more. It lands just days after the Pentagon roughly tripled the ceiling of its main national-security launch programme to $17 billion, naming Rocket Lab as one of only seven eligible providers. Those twin wins come as Rocket Lab also presses ahead with a roughly $8 billion cash-and-stock takeover of satellite operator Iridium, reshaping the Kiwi-founded company into a vertically integrated space powerhouse.
body: Rocket Lab has secured a $266 million firm-fixed-price deal with the U.S. Space Systems Command for 12 suborbital HASTE launches, with options for six more, flying out of the Pacific Spaceport Complex on Kodiak Island, Alaska, through December 2028. The contract beat out two other bidders in a competitive process and builds on a $190 million HASTE block-buy — covering 20 flights — that Rocket Lab signed in March 2026.

The win arrived just days after an even bigger structural shift: in mid-July 2026 the U.S. Space Force roughly tripled the ceiling of its National Security Space Launch Phase 3 Lane 1 contract vehicle, from $5.6 billion to $17 billion, with Rocket Lab named alongside SpaceX, United Launch Alliance, Blue Origin, Stoke Space, Impulse Space and Relativity Federal as one of seven companies eligible to compete for task orders through 2029. The ceiling increase itself obligates no funds until individual missions are competed, but it signals how aggressively the Pentagon is expanding its commercial launch relationships.

HASTE — the Hypersonic Accelerator Suborbital Test Electron — is a modified, suborbital version of Rocket Lab's workhorse Electron rocket, built to test hypersonic technology at speeds faster than Mach 5. Stifel analyst Erik Rasmussen called the Alaska award "strong validation of HASTE's operational performance." The suborbital work also sidesteps a key constraint: Rocket Lab has been on-ramped to the NSSL programme but cannot win its orbital task orders until its new Neutron rocket completes a successful first flight — a hurdle the Alaska missions do not carry.

The defence wins come as Rocket Lab presses ahead with its roughly $8 billion cash-and-stock acquisition of satellite operator Iridium Communications, announced in late June and financed partly through a $3.6 billion bridge loan, which would transform the company from a launch provider into a vertically integrated operator with recurring satellite-service revenue. Rocket Lab reported record first-quarter 2026 revenue of $200.3 million, up 63.5% year-on-year, and exited the quarter with a $2.2 billion backlog — even as its share price has slid well off its late-May record high on investor nerves about the scale and debt load of the Iridium deal.
stories.lens: None of this hardware flies from Māhia, and the defence dollars themselves land in the United States — so the direct benefit to Hawke's Bay is modest and indirect. What matters locally is the balance sheet: a Rocket Lab with a fatter U.S. defence book and recurring satellite revenue from Iridium is a more durable company, and durability is what keeps Launch Complex 1 on the Māhia Peninsula flying and investing in New Zealand engineering and manufacturing roles. For the Bay, the honest play is not to chase the rockets but to build around the anchor: positioning Wairoa and the wider region as the natural home for ground-support, logistics and precision-manufacturing suppliers; pushing councils and iwi land trusts to keep Māhia's access, consents and STEM pathways strong; and helping local agritech and Earth-observation firms learn to buy and use the satellite data this bigger Rocket Lab will increasingly sell — for horticulture, water management and climate resilience. The launch site is a rare asset; capturing value from it takes deliberate regional groundwork, not luck.

stories.headline: New Zealand's rocket launch pad is in Hawke's Bay's backyard
stories.brief: Rocket Lab capped a record year of Electron launches and is targeting the late-2026 debut of Neutron, its larger reusable rocket. Easy to forget behind the Nasdaq listing and US HQ: it launches from Launch Complex 1 at Mahia Peninsula — inside the Hawke's Bay region.
body: Rocket Lab has capped another record run of Electron launches and is closing in on the most important moment in its history: the debut of Neutron, its larger, reusable rocket, targeted for late 2026. Neutron is the vehicle meant to lift the company from small-satellite specialist into serious competition with SpaceX.

It is easy to forget, behind the Nasdaq ticker and the US headquarters, where much of this actually happens. Rocket Lab flies from Launch Complex 1 on the Mahia Peninsula — a windswept spit of land in the Wairoa district, inside the Hawke's Bay region — still the company's original and busiest launch pad.

That makes Hawke's Bay one of the very few places on earth with a working orbital launch site on its doorstep: a magnet for aerospace suppliers, a rare draw for STEM talent, and living proof that globally significant deep-tech can be run from a corner of provincial New Zealand.
stories.lens: Most regions dream of a high-tech anchor; Hawke's Bay already has a working orbital launch site on its doorstep. That is a genuine asset — but proximity alone captures nothing. The concrete opportunity is to turn nearby-ness into supply: local engineering, fabrication, freight and hospitality firms bidding for launch-site work; schools and EIT feeding a STEM and trades pipeline aimed squarely at aerospace; and Wairoa in particular — the district that actually hosts the pad — pressing for its share of the jobs, training and visitor spend rather than watching them route through Auckland or the US HQ. Neutron's arrival will lift Rocket Lab's cadence and profile; the Bay's job is to be organised enough to plug in when it does.

stories.headline: Rocket Lab books its biggest launch deal yet
stories.brief: Rocket Lab announced its largest launch agreement to date — a confidential customer booking multiple Neutron and Electron missions — underlining demand as Neutron nears its debut.
body: Rocket Lab has signed the largest launch contract in its history — a multi-mission deal with an undisclosed customer for five Neutron and three Electron flights between 2026 and 2029. It pushes the company's manifest past 70 missions and its overall backlog beyond US$2.2 billion.

The agreement is a vote of confidence in Neutron, the reusable medium-lift rocket still in development, and the launches will fly from both Launch Complex 1 at Mahia and Launch Complex 3 at Wallops Island in Virginia. It eclipses Rocket Lab's previous 2026 record, a US$190 million hypersonic test deal. "The space industry needs more launch capacity," said founder Sir Peter Beck, "and it needs it from launch providers who know how to deliver."

With 87 Electron launches behind it and more missions sold in the first quarter of 2026 than in all of 2025, Rocket Lab is now the world's second most active launch provider — and a meaningful share of those flights lift off from Hawke's Bay.
stories.lens: Every booked launch is potential work flowing through Māhia and its supply chain — but only if local firms are in a position to win it. The Bay's move is practical: get regional engineering, logistics and services businesses launch-ready and connected to Rocket Lab's procurement, and build the training pipeline so the skilled roles are filled locally rather than imported. The alternative is to keep watching world-class launches lift off from Hawke's Bay soil while the value flies out with them.

sectors.name: Agritech
sectors.tag: Robotics, AI and biotech remaking the primary sector the Bay lives on.

stories.headline: NZ's Gene Tech Bill grinds through Parliament — and Hawke's Bay's orchards and vineyards are watching closely
stories.brief: New Zealand's Gene Technology Bill — which would loosen a near-30-year regime that has effectively kept gene editing out of the field — is grinding through Parliament, but it stalled ahead of its second reading amid coalition negotiations, with New Zealand First withholding support until it is satisfied the rules are safe. Around 15,000 people submitted on the bill, most of them opposed, and the outcome will shape whether fruit, wine and dairy breeders here can use gene-editing tools already embraced in Australia, Japan, the EU and England.
body: New Zealand's gene technology framework is being rewritten for the first time in a generation. Genetically modified organisms are currently regulated under the Hazardous Substances and New Organisms (HSNO) Act 1996, which has effectively confined gene editing to the laboratory, and the replacement Gene Technology Bill — first proposed in late 2024 and written into National's coalition agreements with ACT and New Zealand First — would set up a dedicated regulator to allow wider, controlled use.

That regulator would sit inside the Environmental Protection Authority as a single decision-maker, backed by an administrative office, a Technical Advisory Committee and a Māori Advisory Committee. The Health Select Committee reported the bill back on 10 October 2025, recommending changes before it advances — but progress then stalled ahead of the second reading. Originally intended to pass by the end of 2025, the bill has been held up by coalition negotiations, with New Zealand First's Winston Peters telling supporters it was "going nowhere" unless the party was satisfied it posed no danger.

The debate cuts both ways. ACT wants gene technology liberalised and has objected to the proposed Māori advisory role; Labour's Reuben Davidson warned the bill bundles widely accepted uses like medical research with "far riskier outdoor uses" in a "rushed approach"; and the Greens' Steve Abel cast it as "radical de-regulation" that threatens the GMO-free status New Zealand markets overseas. The organic sector — worth about $1.2 billion — warned that once GMOs are "released there is no containment, no co-existence."

For the primary sector the appeal is faster breeding. The government argues modern gene-editing tools — already used in places like Australia, Japan, the EU and England — could speed the development of disease-resistant, drought-tolerant or higher-yielding plant varieties, precisely the kind of innovation orchards, packhouses and wineries are chasing as climate pressure and labour costs bite. The question the bill has not yet resolved is how to unlock that upside without forfeiting the premium some export buyers pay for GM-free New Zealand produce.
stories.lens: If a workable Gene Technology Bill eventually passes, Hawke's Bay's apple, pear, stonefruit and grape programmes — already leaning on AI and robotics for grading and disease detection — could pair that data with faster, locally bred genetics instead of importing overseas varieties. But the honest picture is unsettled: the bill has stalled, the Māori advisory role and the country's GMO-free marketing edge are still being fought over, and much of the region's export premium rests on a clean, natural story that gene editing could complicate. The practical move for the Bay is to engage now — growers, iwi land trusts and councils should be in the consultation shaping the regulator, and exporters should weigh gene-edited yield gains against the buyers who pay extra precisely because the fruit isn't modified.

stories.headline: A Napier packhouse now runs on AI and robots — and kept all its people
stories.brief: Taylor Corp, a family-owned Napier apple grower more than a century old, rebuilt its packhouse after Cyclone Gabrielle with around $30 million of automation — an AI grader that photographs each apple about 500 times, Aporo sorting robots and driverless forklifts — doubling output to 12,000–14,000 cartons a day while retraining, not replacing, its 80 packhouse staff.
body: When Cyclone Gabrielle tore through Hawke's Bay in early 2023, it destroyed Taylor Corp's Napier packhouse. Rather than rebuild it the way it was, the family-owned apple grower — in business for more than 100 years — spent around $30 million turning it into one of the most automated fruit-packing operations in the country.

At its heart is an AI grader that photographs every apple roughly 500 times as it passes through, spotting splits, stem punctures, black spot and other defects faster and more consistently than a human eye, then sorting fruit by quality and how long it can be stored. Aporo robotic machines place the graded apples onto trays by size and colour, and autonomous mobile robots act as driverless forklifts, using sensors around the shed to learn when pallets are ready to move.

The payoff is scale. The packhouse now pushes out 12,000–14,000 cartons a day — about 3,000 apples a minute, or roughly ten forty-foot shipping containers of export fruit daily — double what it managed before the rebuild. Part-owner Cameron Taylor puts the payback on the technology at about five years, while noting it "goes so quick... it's outdated real quick."

The part Taylor is keenest to stress is what didn't happen: nobody lost their job. The roughly 80 packhouse staff — part of a seasonal workforce of about 400 — were retrained to run and maintain the machines rather than replaced by them. "We've trained them to control the robots so we've actually upskilled them," he told RNZ, turning repetitive line roles into higher-value technical ones.
stories.lens: The template in miniature: import the technology, translate it to a local strength, keep the people and upskill them. It is exactly the kind of move that suits Hawke's Bay, where the bulk of New Zealand's apple crop still has to be graded and packed inside a narrow export window. Multiply Taylor Corp's approach across the Bay's packhouses, coolstores and wineries — pairing capital investment with retraining rather than redundancies — and you have the makings of a regional tech-growth strategy that lifts productivity without hollowing out the local workforce.

stories.headline: Halter's cattle collars now talk to satellites — and that changes hill-country farming
stories.brief: Halter's solar-powered smart collars can now connect direct-to-satellite via Starlink, through One NZ — a world first for virtual fencing — opening the technology to an estimated 20%+ more of New Zealand's beef farms in remote country. It caps a big year: a NZ$377m Series E raise, led by Founders Fund, to fund global expansion.
body: Halter, the New Zealand agritech company whose solar-powered collars let farmers herd and virtually fence cattle from a phone, has removed the one thing that limited where it could work: connectivity. Its collars can now connect direct-to-satellite via Starlink, through One NZ — which Halter says makes it the first company in the world to offer virtual fencing via satellite.

Until now the system needed farm radio towers to reach the collars; Northburn Station in Central Otago, running cattle and merino sheep across 13,000 hectares of high country, would have needed about 25 of them for full coverage. Beaming the link off satellites instead opens the technology to an estimated 20 percent or more of New Zealand's beef farms in remote, broken terrain, and makes Halter the country's largest non-mobile Starlink-connected device provider. "It's not every day you're helping cows connect to satellites in space," said One NZ chief executive Jason Paris.

It caps a landmark year for the company, which in March 2026 raised NZ$377 million in a Series E led by US venture firm Founders Fund — a raise reported at a valuation of around NZ$3.4 billion. Halter already runs collars across New Zealand, Australia and the United States, has passed one million collars sold and 2,000-plus farmers, and is now pushing into the United Kingdom, Ireland and South America. For hill-country farming — long the hardest place to deploy precision tools — satellite is a genuine step change in how stock can be managed, moved and monitored.
stories.lens: Much of the Bay's sheep-and-beef country is exactly the steep, poorly-connected land that couldn't run collars before. Satellite connectivity puts virtual fencing, stock tracking and pasture data within reach of Central Hawke's Bay and the coastal stations — the sort of hill blocks precision farming has always skipped. The concrete opportunity for the region is adoption rather than invention: station owners can now trial virtual fencing without building tower networks, rural contractors and vets could add collar setup and stock-data services, and Gabrielle-damaged fencing lines become less of a barrier to running cattle on broken country.

stories.headline: The first real methane tools hit NZ farms in 2026/27 — here's the shortlist
stories.brief: Several livestock methane tools are nearing market: Ruminant BioTech's rumen bolus (up to 70% cuts for up to six months), BioLumic's UV-treated seed, a methane vaccine (~2028) and Hoofprint's probiotic (up to 80%) — driven by buyers like Tesco, Nestlé and McDonald's demanding lower-emission supply.
body: After years in the lab, the first real tools to cut livestock methane are close to reaching New Zealand paddocks. AgriZeroNZ chief executive Wayne McNee expects several to be available to farmers in 2026/27: Ruminant BioTech's slow-release rumen bolus has shown up to a 70% methane reduction for as long as six months, and BioLumic is using UV-treated seed to lift lipid levels in pasture and lower emissions per kilogram of milksolids.

Others sit a little further out. AgriZeroNZ is backing a methane vaccine — including through US startup ArkeaBio, potentially available around 2028 — US-founded Hoofprint Biome is beginning animal trials of a probiotic targeting reductions of up to 80%, and Agroceutical Products NZ is developing an inhibitor derived from daffodil extract. Breeding lower-methane animals through firms like LIC and CRV adds a slower gain of roughly 1% a year. Together they make New Zealand something of a global testing ground for climate-friendlier cattle.

The pressure driving it all is market access as much as regulation: major buyers including Tesco, Nestlé and McDonald's have ambitious Scope 3 emissions targets and increasingly demand lower-emission supply. Whichever tool clears commercial approval first will start reshaping farm practice — and the premiums attached to it — across sheep-and-beef and dairy country.
stories.lens: For Hawke's Bay's sheep-and-beef and dairy farmers, these tools are less about local invention than about being ready to adopt the first one approved — because the buyers setting the pace (Tesco, Nestlé, McDonald's) feed the same export chains the Bay supplies. The region can't speed up national regulatory approvals, so the honest play is preparation: growers and processors that get early access to a proven tool and can document lower-emission supply stand to protect and lift premiums, while those that wait risk being squeezed out of tightening low-carbon supply contracts. Watching Central Hawke's Bay trial sites and lining up with processors early is the practical move.

stories.headline: The AI that scans 8,000 vines an hour is coming for disease and guesswork
stories.brief: Cropsy mounts AI cameras on vehicles to scan grapevines one by one — around 8,000 an hour — flagging disease, counting vines and estimating yield. It has analysed 22 million vines across NZ, California and Cognac.
body: A New Zealand startup is bringing per-vine intelligence to the vineyard. Cropsy mounts AI cameras on tractors, harvesters, crawlers, ATVs and other vehicles to scan grapevines one at a time — around 8,000 an hour — flagging disease like mildew, counting vines, checking pruning quality and estimating yield, with data back to growers in roughly 30 minutes and typically by the next morning.

Founded out of the University of Auckland's Velocity programme by Leila Deljkovic, the six-year-old company runs a team of about ten and has deployed roughly 40 scanners — mostly across New Zealand but also in California and Cognac, France — analysing some 22 million vines across three continents, 20 million of them in the past year alone. Because contractors can run the scanners, a single unit can cover close to 1,000 hectares for more than 90 growers, putting the technology within reach of small and medium operations.

"We want to fundamentally change how wine grapes are grown, block by block, vine by vine," Deljkovic says — catching disease early, planning picking more precisely, and building the kind of data trail that increasingly matters to premium buyers. Even with a post-Covid squeeze on wine demand, she argues technology like Cropsy's "could turn losses into margins."
stories.lens: Hawke's Bay is New Zealand's second-largest wine region, so per-vine AI is a natural fit: it could catch disease early, sharpen picking decisions and prove sustainability with hard data — an edge as premium buyers demand traceability. The barrier for smaller Bay growers has always been cost, and Cropsy's contractor model — one scanner covering close to 1,000 hectares for dozens of growers — is exactly what lowers it. The concrete opportunity is a shared, contractor-run scanning service across the region's vineyards, turning per-vine data into earlier disease control and a credible sustainability story for export.

stories.headline: A Hawke's Bay apple just signed one of China's biggest stars
stories.brief: Rockit — the snack-sized apple pioneered in Hawke's Bay around 20 years ago as the world's first miniature apple — has signed Chinese superstar Wang Yibo as brand ambassador to drive sales in China, the world's largest apple market. It now sells across 30+ territories and grows in eight regions worldwide.
body: Rockit, the snack-sized apple pioneered in Hawke's Bay around 20 years ago as the world's first miniature apple, has landed a marketing coup: it has signed Chinese superstar Wang Yibo — an actor, singer, dancer and motorsport competitor, and previously a face for Chanel and Lacoste — as brand ambassador to drive sales in China, the world's largest and most dynamic apple market, from May 2026.

The company now sells in more than 30 territories and grows across eight regions worldwide to keep year-round supply, all from a brand that began as one small New Zealand apple. Rockit Global chief executive Grant McBeath said partnering with an ambassador of Wang's calibre was "a powerful way to reach new audiences at scale," and significant for any brand, "let alone one from a small market like New Zealand," noting that around 80 percent of people who try the apple go on to repurchase it.

Rockit's story is less about fruit than about intellectual property, branding and marketing muscle exported from the Bay to the world — a template other regional food producers are studying as they look to capture value beyond the raw commodity.
stories.lens: Rockit turned a small Bay apple into a global premium brand — proof the region can export IP, branding and marketing muscle, not just fruit. The lesson for other Hawke's Bay food producers is that the value sits in the brand and the repeat customer, not the raw crop: the same playbook of a protected variety, tight quality control and serious offshore marketing could work for the Bay's stonefruit, wine or specialty produce. The practical question for growers and investors here is whether to keep selling commodities or to build the brand and distribution muscle that captures the margin Rockit has shown is on the table.

sectors.name: The Bay Scene
sectors.tag: Tech and innovation happening right here in Hawke’s Bay.

stories.headline: Hawke's Bay drone firm lands NZ-first certification — and a $60m Australasia distribution deal
stories.brief: Hawke's Bay-based Aerospread Technologies has a New Zealand first: its xFold H500 heavy-lift drone (200kg payload) is the first aircraft of its class to win full CAA Part 102 certification for unrestricted agricultural operations in New Zealand. The milestone was revealed alongside a distribution deal in which US-based Powerus, via subsidiary Kaizen Aerospace, named the Napier company its exclusive agent for the xFold platform across Australia, New Zealand and the South Pacific — with performance-based targets of about $60 million in product revenue over five years (targets, not binding orders).
body: A locally built aviation story just went global. Aerospread Technologies, which operates from a purpose-built facility in Hawke's Bay, has notched a genuine New Zealand first: its xFold H500, a 200kg-payload heavy-lift drone, is now the first aircraft of its class to receive full CAA Part 102 certification for unrestricted agricultural operations in New Zealand — clearing a regulatory bar that has held back large autonomous ag-aircraft.

The certification was revealed alongside a major commercial deal. US-based Autonomous Power Corporation, trading as Powerus and based in West Palm Beach, Florida, announced that its wholly owned subsidiary Kaizen Aerospace had launched a dedicated agriculture division and appointed Aerospread Technologies as its exclusive agent for xFold sales and distribution across the Australia and New Zealand markets and the wider South Pacific. Based on Aerospread's projected volumes, the sales targets represent roughly $60 million in potential product revenue over the first five years — though the companies stress these are performance objectives, not binding purchase commitments.

The same announcement revealed a parallel US arrangement. Benton, Kentucky-based Sprig Aerospace became an authorised distributor and marketing partner that will standardise its commercial spraying and aerial-application fleet on Powerus xFold aircraft, and the FAA issued Sprig a Special Airworthiness Certificate (Experimental Category), plus a Certificate of Waiver of Authorization, for the larger xFold Dragon H1000 for research and development. That places the Hawke's Bay operation at the centre of an international rollout of heavy-lift agricultural drone technology, rather than a bit-part local supply arrangement.

Aerospread, founded in 2017 by veteran agricultural pilot Bruce Peterson, has grown from a topdressing operator into a manufacturer and technology developer in its own right, running its aerial services under the Aerotech UAV brand while Aerospread Technologies Ltd drives the innovation, manufacturing and certification work behind it.
stories.lens: This is a rare case of a Hawke's Bay-headquartered company setting the pace rather than adopting someone else's technology — the CAA Part 102 milestone was won on home soil, at a Hawke's Bay facility, before the company was handed distribution rights spanning Australia, New Zealand and the South Pacific. To build on it, the region could keep the high-value engineering, flight-testing and regulatory work anchored locally rather than letting it drift offshore as the deal scales; grow a supply chain of drone technicians, remote pilots and maintenance crews through local training providers and the Hi-Tech Hawke's Bay network; and get growers trialling heavy-lift autonomous spraying and spreading on the orchard, vineyard and steep forestry blocks where labour is scarcest. Positioning the Bay as New Zealand's proving ground for large agricultural UAVs — with councils and investors backing the certification and testing capability that already sits here — is how a single world-class win becomes a durable local cluster.

stories.headline: The Bay quietly built a food-innovation campus — and it's filling up
stories.brief: Foodeast Haumako, a purpose-built food, beverage and agritech innovation centre at Tomoana, Hastings, offers 600m² production and warehouse bays, office tenancies, meeting and conference space, and a startup-support model — and already houses businesses including Mara Bio, AsureQuality and the New Zealand Food Innovation Network.
body: Hawke's Bay has quietly built itself a home for food innovation. Foodeast Haumako, a purpose-built food, beverage and agritech innovation centre at 4 Hanui Road, Tomoana, Hastings, sets out to be "New Zealand's leading catalyser of commercially successful food innovation" — offering the physical and commercial scaffolding local makers have long lacked.

The site pairs light-filled office tenancies of varying sizes with four 600-square-metre production and warehouse bays, two tech-forward meeting rooms, a boardroom and a dedicated conference space, plus an action-oriented startup-support model. It already houses businesses including Mara Bio, AsureQuality, the New Zealand Food Innovation Network and the Bioresource Processing Alliance, and runs a "Sustainable is Attainable" programme aimed at developing viable alternatives for the waste and by-products generated during food processing and manufacturing.

For a region that grows an enormous volume of raw product but has often watched the value-add happen elsewhere, a place to prototype, scale and commercialise without leaving the Bay is exactly the missing piece.
stories.lens: This is the physical backbone the region's foodtech ambitions have lacked — somewhere Bay growers and makers can prototype, scale and commercialise without shipping the value-add out of the province. To push the momentum further, the priority is simple: fill the bays with local ventures moving beyond raw commodity, and wire the campus tightly into the region's growers and processors so more of the margin is captured here. The "Sustainable is Attainable" stream is a concrete lever — turning packhouse and processing waste into saleable products — while councils and investors could back tenancy incentives and shared-equipment access so early-stage food ventures can reach commercial scale without leaving Hawke's Bay.

stories.headline: Napier Port bets up to $25m on self-driving trucks — a first for NZ ports
stories.brief: Napier Port plans a fleet of about a dozen battery-electric autonomous trucks to move containers around its terminal — an investment estimated at $20–25 million, a first for a New Zealand port. The Maritime Union has warned the automation is "a threat to jobs, safety, and productivity."
body: Napier Port is preparing to become the first port in New Zealand to run a fleet of autonomous trucks. The plan, estimated at $20–25 million including a battery-swap station, would put about a dozen battery-electric self-driving vehicles to work loading and shifting containers within the container terminal. The first truck was due to arrive from China in the first half of 2026, with the rest of the fleet later in the year. The port frames it as a productivity and safety upgrade — pairing the fleet with a new one-way traffic system it says will cut the major risk of vehicle collision — for the Bay's main export gateway, a company majority-owned by the Hawke's Bay Regional Council.

It hasn't landed without friction. The Maritime Union of New Zealand pushed back on 26 September 2025, with national secretary Carl Findlay calling the move "a threat to jobs, safety, and productivity across the sector" and pointing to Ports of Auckland's abandoned automated straddle-carrier programme in 2022 as a cautionary tale. The port has acknowledged the shift will bring a small number of redundancies among heavy-plant operators, while noting new roles are emerging — 11 staff are already completing an electric-vehicle engineering certificate.

That tension is the story. Napier Port is the route to market for the region's apples, wine, timber and squash, so anything that makes it faster and more competitive matters — but so do the port jobs that come with it. It is precisely the kind of shift that reads differently through a Hawke's Bay lens than a national one.
stories.lens: The Bay's export gateway going automated is a genuinely two-sided local story — competitiveness on one hand, port jobs on the other. Because Napier Port is majority-owned by the Hawke's Bay Regional Council, the region has real leverage to shape a just transition: redeploy and retrain displaced heavy-plant operators into the EV-engineering, maintenance and control-room roles the new fleet creates (the 11 staff already on an EV certificate are the model), and make sure the productivity gains flow back into the regional economy rather than out of it. Getting the union, the port and the council around the same table early is how the Bay captures the efficiency without hollowing out the workforce that depends on it.

stories.headline: Hi-tech is quietly blossoming across Hawke's Bay
stories.brief: Beyond the headline names, a growing base of tech firms is taking root across the Bay — just under 500 firms in high-tech manufacturing and ICT, employing more than 1,500 people, with the Hi-Tech Hawke's Bay network alone counting around 240 members.
body: Beneath the headline names, Hawke's Bay has grown a surprisingly deep tech base. The region is now home to just under 500 firms across high-tech manufacturing and ICT, employing more than 1,500 people, and the Hi-Tech Hawke's Bay network alone counts around 240 members.

The roster runs well beyond Rocket Lab: Fingermark, software firms like Re-leased and Ask Your Team, StockX, agri-data players HortPlus and MyEnviro, and automation specialists such as MHM Automation, CR Automation and RBE Hortworx — alongside big local names Pan Pac and Napier Port. Xero founder Rod Drury keeps an office in the Ahuriri Tech Collective, a shared workspace whose tenants include NOW, WebFox and Re-leased and which has become a hub for the scene.

Under it sits a talent pipeline: the iwi-led Puhoro STEM programme, which began delivering in Hawke's Bay in 2021 and has supported dozens of rangatahi into tech skills, and a Rocket Lab education centre coming to Wairoa backed by a $6 million Provincial Growth Fund grant. "It's hard to define tech as one thing," says Hi-Tech Hawke's Bay chair Dave France. "We're moving fast as a region and even the most traditional industries are using or developing digital capabilities in some form or another." Surfacing and connecting these firms is exactly how a scattered scene becomes an ecosystem.
stories.lens: This is the grassroots the region's tech-growth story is built on — a scene, not yet fully an ecosystem. The concrete moves that would push the momentum further are unglamorous but real: keep surfacing and connecting the firms so they can share talent, tooling and customers rather than compete blind; feed the talent pipeline by scaling Puhoro STEM and the Wairoa education centre so young Māori and rural students have a genuine local path into tech; and lean on models like the Ahuriri Tech Collective — plus remote-work-friendly lifestyle — to keep graduates in the Bay and draw others back. A region that deliberately stitches 500 scattered firms into a network is how the province claims its share of the national tech boom.
